name: Numbering concordance — Douay-Rheims / Vulgate to modern Catholic numbering
purpose: The Catholic Cross References dataset is keyed to the Douay-Rheims (Vulgate) book names and numbering, because that is the text its evidence was verified against. Cross references themselves are passage-to-passage and translation-independent; this file is the bridge that lets a project using modern Catholic numbering (as in the NABRE or RSV-CE) translate the dataset's references into its own. It is a chapter-level concordance: where verse numbering also shifts, the note says so, and the passage should be located by its words.
license: Public domain (Unlicense) — the correspondences themselves are centuries-old facts of the biblical text.

book_names.note: Douay-Rheims name -> the name in modern Catholic Bibles. Books not listed keep the same name in both (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Judges, Ruth, Job, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Wisdom, Jeremias's Lamentations and Baruch, the twelve minor prophets not listed, the four Gospels by evangelist, and all the epistles).

psalms.note: Vulgate psalm -> modern psalm. The two numberings share one text; they part where the Hebrew and Greek traditions divide or join psalms differently. Four places differ structurally: Vulgate 9 joins modern 9 and 10; Vulgate 113 joins modern 114 and 115; Vulgate 114 and 115 divide modern 116 between them; Vulgate 146 and 147 divide modern 147. Between those places the modern number runs one ahead of the Vulgate. Verse numbering inside a psalm can also shift by a verse where one tradition counts the psalm's title inscription as verse 1 and the other does not (notably Psalms 51-... in Vulgate numbering, e.g. Vulgate 50, 21, 68) — locate by the words when a verse seems off by one.

esther.note: The Douay-Rheims prints the Greek additions to Esther as its own chapters 11-16 (and extra verses at the end of chapter 10). Modern Catholic Bibles print the same material as lettered Additions A-F, placed inside the story. The arrangement below is the standard one (as in the NABRE and RSV-CE); the verse division of Addition D varies slightly by edition.

A.placement: before 1:1 — the dream of Mardochai, and the eunuchs' plot

B.placement: after 3:13 — the king's letter ordering the destruction

C.placement: after 4:17 — the prayers of Mardochai and of Esther

D.placement: at 5:1 — Esther goes in to the king

E.placement: after 8:12 — the king's second letter, undoing the first

F.placement: after 10:3, at the end of the book — the interpretation of Mardochai's dream

daniel.note: The Douay-Rheims Daniel carries the Greek portions inside the book. Modern Catholic Bibles keep the same arrangement with one renumbering inside chapter 3.

prayer_and_song_in_chapter_3.modern: chapter 3, inserted between verses 23 and 24 (the Prayer of Azarias, 3:24-50, and the Song of the Three Children, 3:51-90); the verses after the insertion keep roughly parallel numbers to the end of the chapter (100 verses in the Douay-Rheims), with small differences by edition

other_notes: Ecclesiasticus (Sirach): chapter numbering agrees; verse numbering inside some chapters (notably in the 30s) differs between editions following different Greek traditions. Locate by the words.

Jeremias (Jeremiah): in the Douay-Rheims, Baruch's letter (the Letter of Jeremiah) is Baruch chapter 6; some modern editions print it as a separate short book after Lamentations or as Baruch 6 — same text.

In a handful of New Testament places the Douay-Rheims versification runs one verse off from modern editions (for example the didrachma passage in Matthew 17); the dataset's references follow the Douay-Rheims text they were verified against.
